title: JSON to CSV & CSV to JSON Converter - Free & Private
description: Convert JSON to CSV or CSV to JSON instantly in your browser. Handles headers, quotes, commas and multiline values without uploads.

directions.summary: Turn a JSON object or object array into CSV with a header row.
Parse a header-based CSV document into a JSON object array.

faq.q: Can I convert CSV to JSON on the same page?
faq.a: Yes. Enter content in either fixed-format editor and use the direction buttons between them without opening another page.

faq.q: Does the converter support commas and newlines?
faq.a: Yes. Properly quoted CSV fields can contain commas, double quotes and line breaks.

faq.q: Is my data uploaded to a server?
faq.a: No. All conversion happens in your browser memory. Nothing is sent, stored or logged on a server.

faq.q: What is the maximum CSV file size?
faq.a: The limit is your device memory. Most browsers handle files of several megabytes instantly; very large files may take a moment but still never leave your computer.

faq.q: Does it handle nested JSON objects?
faq.a: Yes. Nested objects and arrays are serialized as JSON text inside the CSV cell so the data is preserved. Flatten the JSON first if you need each key as its own column.

faq.q: Can I download the result?
faq.a: Yes. Use the Download button to save the converted output as a file with the matching extension.

content.heading: How to convert JSON to CSV
body: Paste a JSON object or an array of objects into the input field and the converter writes a CSV document with one header row followed by one row per record. The tool reads the keys of the first object to build the header, so every object should share the same structure for a clean spreadsheet.

Nested objects and arrays are serialized as JSON strings inside the cell, which keeps CSV flat and importable by Excel, Google Sheets and database loaders. To produce a tidy table, flatten deeply nested JSON before converting.

content.heading: CSV quoting and special characters
body: RFC 4180 quoting is applied automatically: any field that contains a comma, double quote or line break is wrapped in double quotes, and embedded double quotes are escaped by doubling them. This means multiline values and values with commas survive a round trip back to JSON without corruption.

The parser handles both 
 and 
 line endings and trims no data, so values are preserved exactly as written.

content.heading: When to use CSV instead of JSON
body: CSV is ideal when you need a tabular, human-readable format for spreadsheets, data exchange with legacy systems or bulk database imports. JSON is better for nested or hierarchical data. Converting between the two lets you move records between APIs and spreadsheet workflows without losing structure.

title: Base64 Encode & Decode Online - UTF-8 and Private
description: Encode text to Base64 or decode Base64 to UTF-8 locally in your browser. Free, instant and no uploads.

directions.summary: Encode UTF-8 text as standard Base64.
Decode standard Base64 into readable UTF-8 text.

faq.q: Is Base64 encoding encryption?
faq.a: No. Base64 is a reversible text encoding and should not be used to protect secrets.

faq.q: Can this tool decode UTF-8 text?
faq.a: Yes. The decoder validates the Base64 input and returns UTF-8 text.

faq.q: Does it support UTF-8 and emoji?
faq.a: Yes. Text is encoded as UTF-8 before Base64, so emoji, CJK characters and other non-ASCII text round-trip correctly.

faq.q: Is Base64 secure?
faq.a: No. Base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode it, so never use it to protect secrets or passwords.

faq.q: Why is the encoded text longer?
faq.a: Base64 turns every three bytes into four characters, so encoded output is about 33% larger than the original binary data.

faq.q: Can I encode images or binary files?
faq.a: This tool encodes text. For binary files, convert them to Base64 in your application using the platform's built-in APIs.

content.heading: What is Base64 encoding
body: Base64 encodes binary or text data into a 64-character alphabet (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, + and /) so it can travel safely through text-only channels such as email, JSON, URL query strings and data URIs. Every three bytes of input become four Base64 characters, which is why encoded output is about one third larger than the original.
This converter uses standard UTF-8 encoding, so non-ASCII characters like emoji and CJK text round-trip correctly without mojibake.

content.heading: Encoding vs encryption
body: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode it, so never use it to protect secrets or passwords. Its purpose is transport safety, not confidentiality. For security, combine Base64 transport with a real encryption layer such as AES.

content.heading: Common Base64 use cases
body: Embed images and fonts as data URIs in CSS and HTML, store small binary blobs inside JSON or YAML configuration, transfer credentials in HTTP Basic authentication headers, and attach files in MIME email. Each of these channels only reliably handles text, so Base64 bridges binary data into them.

title: JSON to YAML & YAML to JSON Converter - Online & Private
description: Convert JSON to YAML or YAML to JSON on one private browser page. Supports nested objects and arrays without uploads.

directions.summary: Convert JSON configuration into readable YAML.
Parse YAML configuration into formatted JSON.

faq.q: Can I convert YAML back to JSON here?
faq.a: Yes. Enter YAML in its editor and use the YAML-to-JSON direction button on this same canonical page.

faq.q: Does this JSON YAML converter upload my configuration?
faq.a: No. Parsing and serialization run entirely inside your browser.

faq.q: Is YAML a superset of JSON?
faq.a: Yes. Every valid JSON document is also valid YAML, which is why conversion between them is lossless and reversible.

faq.q: Does it preserve key order?
faq.a: Yes. Keys keep their original order from the JSON, so the YAML output matches your source document structure.

faq.q: Can YAML have comments?
faq.a: Yes, YAML supports comments with # while JSON does not. Converting JSON to YAML lets you add documentation to machine-generated configuration.

faq.q: Does it handle nested objects and arrays?
faq.a: Yes. Nested objects become indented mappings and arrays become dash-prefixed list items, preserving the full hierarchy.

content.heading: How JSON maps to YAML
body: YAML is a superset of JSON, so every valid JSON document is also valid YAML. This converter turns JSON braces and brackets into clean YAML indentation, producing configuration that is easier to read and edit by hand for Kubernetes manifests, CI pipelines and application settings.
Nested objects become indented mappings, arrays become dash-prefixed list items, and strings are emitted without quotes whenever it is safe to do so.

content.heading: YAML formatting conventions
body: The output uses two-space indentation and folds long JSON onto readable lines. Keys keep their original order, and null values render as the bare word null. Booleans and numbers are typed exactly like JSON, so types round-trip correctly when you convert back.

content.heading: Choosing YAML for configuration
body: YAML shines for human-edited configuration because it supports comments, multiline strings and anchors, which JSON does not. Converting JSON to YAML lets you take machine-generated configuration and add documentation and structure before committing it to a repository.

title: JSON to XML & XML to JSON Converter - Safe and Private
description: Convert JSON to XML or XML to JSON locally. Supports attributes, text and repeated elements while rejecting unsafe entity declarations.

directions.summary: Create XML from JSON using @ attributes and #text values.
Parse safe XML into JSON with predictable attribute and array mapping.

faq.q: How are XML attributes represented in JSON?
faq.a: Attribute names use an @ prefix, text uses #text and repeated elements become arrays.

faq.q: Does the XML parser load external entities?
faq.a: No. DOCTYPE and ENTITY declarations are rejected before parsing.

faq.q: Is it safe against XXE attacks?
faq.a: Yes. The parser rejects external entity declarations and document type definitions, so untrusted input cannot access the file system or network.

faq.q: Does it support repeated elements as arrays?
faq.a: Yes. Repeated child elements with the same name are mapped to a JSON array, and single elements map to an object.

faq.q: Can I round-trip between JSON and XML?
faq.a: Yes. Using the @ attribute and #text conventions, data converts back and forth without losing metadata or structure.

content.heading: Converting JSON to XML
body: JSON objects become XML elements, object keys become element names, and arrays become repeated child elements. To express XML attributes, the converter follows the @-prefix convention: a key named @id becomes an attribute id on the element, while #text sets the element's text content.
This mapping keeps the conversion lossless and reversible, so you can round-trip between JSON and XML without dropping metadata.

content.heading: Safe XML parsing
body: The parser rejects dangerous constructs such as external entity declarations (XXE) and document type definitions, which are a common source of XML security vulnerabilities. Only well-formed elements, attributes and text are accepted, so untrusted input cannot reach the file system or the network.

content.heading: JSON vs XML for data exchange
body: XML is still required by SOAP services, legacy enterprise systems and many document standards. JSON is lighter and dominates modern APIs. Converting between them lets an XML-based system consume JSON payloads and vice versa without manual rewriting.

title: Unix Timestamp to Date & Date to Timestamp Converter
description: Convert Unix timestamps in seconds or milliseconds to UTC ISO dates, or convert ISO DateTime back to Unix seconds.

directions.summary: Detect Unix seconds or milliseconds and display an ISO 8601 UTC date.
Convert an ISO 8601 date and time into Unix seconds.

faq.q: Does the timestamp converter accept milliseconds?
faq.a: Yes. Large numeric values are automatically interpreted as milliseconds; shorter values are treated as seconds.

faq.q: Which timezone is shown?
faq.a: Timestamp results use UTC and the ISO 8601 format ending in Z.

faq.q: What is the Unix epoch?
faq.a: The Unix epoch is 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. A Unix timestamp counts the seconds elapsed since that moment and is independent of timezones.

faq.q: Does it detect seconds vs milliseconds?
faq.a: Yes. The converter recognizes whether your input is in seconds or milliseconds based on its magnitude, which is useful for JavaScript and Java timestamps.

faq.q: Which timezone is used?
faq.a: All conversions use UTC, the same reference as the Unix epoch. The ISO 8601 output ends with Z to mark UTC explicitly.

faq.q: Can I convert an ISO date back to a timestamp?
faq.a: Yes. Paste an ISO 8601 date and time to get the equivalent Unix timestamp in seconds.

content.heading: Understanding Unix timestamps
body: A Unix timestamp counts the seconds that have elapsed since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, known as the Unix epoch. It is timezone-independent and used everywhere from databases and logs to cache headers and cron jobs. This converter detects whether your input is in seconds or milliseconds automatically.
Because the value is a plain number, timestamps sort naturally and avoid the ambiguity of localized date strings.

content.heading: Converting in both directions
body: Paste a numeric timestamp to see the equivalent ISO 8601 UTC date and time, or paste an ISO 8601 date to get the Unix seconds back. Millisecond timestamps, common in JavaScript and Java, are recognised when the magnitude falls in the millisecond range.

content.heading: Timezone and ISO 8601 notes
body: All conversions use UTC, the same reference as the Unix epoch. To display a local time, convert the timestamp in your application using its own timezone rules. ISO 8601 output includes the trailing Z to mark UTC explicitly.

title: JSON to Go Struct Converter - Free & Private
description: Convert JSON objects into typed Go structs instantly in your browser. Free, private, and no signup required.

directions.summary: Generate typed Go structs with JSON field tags.

faq.q: Does this JSON to Go converter upload my data?
faq.a: No. Conversion runs entirely in your browser, so your JSON never leaves your device.

faq.q: How are nested objects handled?
faq.a: Nested JSON objects become named Go structs and arrays receive inferred element types.

faq.q: What Go types are inferred?
faq.a: Strings map to string, numbers to float64, booleans to bool and arrays to slices. Nested objects become referenced struct types with json tags.

faq.q: Does it generate json tags?
faq.a: Yes. Each field gets a json tag that preserves the original JSON key, so encoding/json deserializes your payload without manual mapping.

faq.q: Can I use the structs with encoding/json?
faq.a: Yes. Pass a value of the root struct to json.Unmarshal and the tags handle the key mapping automatically.

content.heading: Generating Go structs from JSON
body: Paste a JSON object and the converter emits a set of typed Go structs, one per nested object, with field names exported in PascalCase and json tags that preserve the original keys. This matches the convention used by the encoding/json package, so the generated code deserializes your payload without extra mapping.
Arrays become slices, nested objects become referenced struct types, and null values are handled with pointer or omitempty-friendly tagging.

content.heading: Type inference rules
body: Numbers become float64 by default, the type encoding/json uses during generic decoding. Booleans map to bool, strings to string, and arrays to []T. When you need int or a specific width, adjust the generated field type after pasting.

content.heading: Integrating with your Go project
body: Copy the generated structs into a models package and pass a value of the root struct to json.Unmarshal. Because the json tags match your API keys exactly, you avoid manual field-by-field mapping and can evolve the types as the schema changes.

title: JSON to TypeScript Interface Converter
description: Generate clean TypeScript interfaces from JSON locally in your browser, with nested object and array support.

directions.summary: Generate clean TypeScript interfaces from JSON.

faq.q: Can this converter infer nested TypeScript interfaces?
faq.a: Yes. Nested objects generate separate interfaces and arrays infer their element types.

faq.q: Is the generated TypeScript editable?
faq.a: Yes. Copy or download the output and adapt the generated interfaces in your project.

faq.q: Does it mark optional fields?
faq.a: Yes. Fields that are null or missing in the JSON are marked optional, so the types reflect real API responses that may omit keys.

faq.q: How are nested objects named?
faq.a: Each nested object is promoted to its own interface, named after its parent key in PascalCase to keep deeply nested payloads readable.

faq.q: Can I paste the output into a .ts file?
faq.a: Yes. The output is idiomatic TypeScript with imports and is ready to paste directly into your project.

faq.q: Does it work with arrays?
faq.a: Yes. JSON arrays become T[] syntax with the correct element type inferred from the data.

content.heading: Generating TypeScript interfaces from JSON
body: Paste a JSON object and the converter produces clean, idiomatic TypeScript interfaces, one per nested object, with descriptive names derived from the keys. Arrays become T[], optional fields are marked, and the output is ready to paste directly into a .ts file.
The generated types let the compiler catch spelling mistakes and schema drift at build time instead of at runtime.

content.heading: Naming and nesting
body: Each nested object is promoted to its own interface and named after its parent key in PascalCase, which keeps deeply nested payloads readable. Union types and optional members are inferred when a field is null or missing, so the types reflect real API responses.

content.heading: Using the generated types
body: Add the interfaces to your project and annotate fetch or API client calls with them. Pair the types with a runtime validator such as zod when you consume untrusted data, so both compile-time and runtime safety are covered.

title: JSON to Python Dataclass Generator
description: Turn JSON objects into typed Python dataclasses in your browser, including nested models and lists.

directions.summary: Generate typed Python dataclasses from JSON.

faq.q: Which Python version does the output target?
faq.a: The generated code uses standard dataclasses and built-in generic types available in modern Python 3.

faq.q: How are invalid Python field names handled?
faq.a: Field names are sanitized and a metadata mapping preserves the original JSON key.

faq.q: Does it use the @dataclass decorator?
faq.a: Yes. Each generated class uses the @dataclass decorator with standard typing imports, so __init__, __repr__ and equality are generated for free.

faq.q: How are lists typed?
faq.a: Arrays become list[T] with the element type inferred, matching modern Python typing conventions.

faq.q: Are nested objects supported?
faq.a: Yes. Nested objects become their own dataclasses referenced by name, keeping structured payloads organized.

faq.q: How do I load JSON into the dataclasses?
faq.a: Parse the JSON with json.loads and construct the root class, or use a library like dacite or pydantic to populate nested fields automatically.

content.heading: Generating Python dataclasses from JSON
body: Paste a JSON object and the converter emits typed Python dataclasses, including nested classes for nested objects and lists with element types. The output uses the @dataclass decorator and standard typing imports, so it works with both dataclasses and modern type checkers.
Because dataclasses generate __init__, __repr__ and equality for free, you get value objects that are easy to construct, compare and log.

content.heading: Type annotations and nesting
body: Strings map to str, numbers to float, booleans to bool, and arrays to list[T]. Nested objects become their own dataclasses referenced by name, which keeps deeply structured payloads organized across multiple classes instead of one flat dictionary.

content.heading: Loading JSON into dataclasses
body: After pasting the dataclasses, parse the JSON with json.loads and construct the root class, or use a library like dacite or pydantic to populate nested fields automatically. This turns raw dictionaries into objects with attribute access and type checking.

title: JSON to Rust Struct Generator
description: Generate serde-ready Rust structs from JSON locally, with nested objects, vectors, and renamed fields.

directions.summary: Generate serde-ready Rust structs from JSON.

faq.q: Does the output work with serde?
faq.a: Yes. Generated structs derive Serialize and Deserialize and add rename attributes when required.

faq.q: What type is used for JSON numbers?
faq.a: Integers use i64 and decimal values use f64.

faq.q: Does it add serde derive attributes?
faq.a: Yes. The output includes serde derive macros and rename rules so the structs deserialize directly with serde_json::from_str.

faq.q: How are optional fields handled?
faq.a: Fields that can be null become Option<T>, and arrays become Vec<T>, matching how serde models real-world data.

faq.q: Does it use rename rules?
faq.a: Yes. serde rename_all rules like camelCase or snake_case are applied so JSON keys map to idiomatic Rust field names without per-field attributes.

faq.q: Can I use it with serde_json?
faq.a: Yes. Add serde and serde_json to Cargo.toml and call serde_json::from_str on the generated root type.

content.heading: Generating serde-ready Rust structs
body: Paste a JSON object and the converter emits Rust structs with serde derive attributes and rename rules that keep the original JSON keys. The output is ready for serde_json::from_str, so you can deserialize API payloads into strongly typed values with compile-time guarantees.
Optional fields become Option<T>, arrays become Vec<T>, and nested objects become referenced structs, matching how serde models real-world data.

content.heading: Rename rules and field mapping
body: serde's rename_all = "camelCase" or "snake_case" rules are applied so that idiomatic JSON keys map to idiomatic Rust field names without per-field attributes. This keeps the generated code concise even for large payloads.

content.heading: Integrating with a Rust project
body: Add serde and serde_json to Cargo.toml, paste the structs into a module, and call serde_json::from_str::<RootType>(&payload). The compiler then verifies every field access, eliminating a whole class of runtime key errors.
